summary.text: Supersaturation occurs when a solution holds more solute than its solubility at equilibrium allows.
Such a solution is in a metastable state and can return to equilibrium by separating out the excess solute, by dilution, or by increasing the solute's solubility.
Crystals may be slow to form because of a thermodynamic barrier, which adding a tiny crystal of the solute commonly overcomes.

facts.value: Adding a tiny crystal of the solute to start crystals forming

facts.value: Sodium sulfate, also known as Glauber's Salt

items.prompt: A liquid has gas dissolved in it while the gas is pressed hard against it. The pressure is then eased off. How does the liquid's capacity for that gas change?

options.label: It drops, since gas solubility rises with gas pressure
It grows, since less pressure lets more gas in
It stays fixed, since pressure only affects solids
It vanishes, since gas never stays dissolved in liquid

items.explain: The solubility of a gas in a liquid increases with increasing gas pressure, so easing the pressure lowers what the liquid can hold.

items.prompt: A chemist heats an impure compound in a solvent until it dissolves, then cools it. What happens as it cools?

options.label: It stays fully dissolved, and the impurities are what form the crystals
It briefly becomes supersaturated, then crystals form and impurities stay in the liquid
It evaporates away, leaving the impurities behind as a gas
It turns into a gas while only the impurities crystallize out

items.explain: On cooling, the solution briefly becomes supersaturated and the compound crystallizes out, while impurities remain in the supernatant liquid.

items.prompt: A cooled solution stays clear though it holds extra solute. A chemist drops in a tiny crystal of the solute. Why?

options.label: The crystal cools the solution down much further
The crystal dilutes the solution it is added to
The crystal gives crystals a place to start, overcoming the barrier
The crystal adds extra solvent to the solution

items.explain: Seeding with a tiny crystal helps overcome the thermodynamic barrier to forming a crystal, acting as a starting site.

items.prompt: Some carbohydrate solutions stay supersaturated for a long time. What keeps them from crystallizing?

options.label: Their molecules are too small to bond with water
Their crystals dissolve faster than they form
They contain too little solute to ever crystallize
Extensive, irregular hydrogen bonding with water makes the barrier high

items.explain: The thermodynamic barrier to crystal formation is rather high for carbohydrates because of extensive and irregular hydrogen bonding with the solvent, water.

items.prompt: When a saturated solution is cooled, what usually happens to the excess solute?

options.label: Solubility rises, so it dissolves even faster
Solubility drops, so it rapidly separates as crystals or powder
It turns into a gas
It sinks and becomes a solvent

items.explain: In most cases solubility decreases with decreasing temperature, so the excess of solute rapidly separates as crystals or an amorphous powder.

items.prompt: A solution has stopped forming new crystals but is still supersaturated. How do the crystals already there get bigger?

options.label: They merge with one another into larger crystals
They melt the solvent around them to make room
They take in more solute by diffusion
They push the extra solute out as a gas

items.explain: Once the supersaturation is too low for new crystals to nucleate, the existing crystals grow by solute diffusion because the solution is still supersaturated.

paragraphs.heading: More dissolved than should fit
paragraphs.text: Supersaturation is the state of a solution that holds more dissolved substance than its solubility at equilibrium allows. The dissolved substance is called the solute. The word is used most often for a solid dissolved in a liquid. It can also describe liquids or gases dissolved in a liquid.

paragraphs.heading: An uneasy balance
paragraphs.text: A supersaturated solution is metastable: it can stay as it is for a while, but it is not truly settled. It can get back to equilibrium in three ways. The extra solute can come out of the solution, more solvent can be added to dilute it, or the solute can be made more soluble. In some cases crystals are slow to appear, and the solution stays supersaturated after it cools. The cause is a thermodynamic barrier to forming a crystal in a liquid. Chemists usually get past it by dropping in a tiny crystal of the same compound, which is called seeding, or by rubbing a rod on the glass so that microscopic glass bits break off and give crystals a place to start.

paragraphs.heading: Made by changing temperature
paragraphs.text: Changing the temperature of a saturated solution can make it supersaturated. For most substances, solubility falls as the temperature falls, so the excess soon comes out as crystals or as a shapeless powder. A few substances behave the other way round. Sodium sulfate, also called Glauber's salt, is the well-known case: above 33 °C it dissolves less in water as the water gets hotter. That odd behavior is why early researchers chose it.

paragraphs.heading: What starts a crystal
paragraphs.text: Early work showed that shaking a supersaturated solution is not what makes it crystallize, as people had believed. Instead, bits of solid matter that get in act as starting points for crystals, now called seeds. Henri Löwel later concluded that both nuclei in the solution and the walls of the container help set off crystallization. Désiré Gernez then found that the nuclei must be the same salt that is crystallizing.

paragraphs.heading: LaMer's three stages
paragraphs.text: In 1950, Victor K. LaMer put forward a model of how crystals begin and grow. First, solute builds up steadily in the solution. When it passes the saturation level, nothing comes out at once; the solution keeps taking in solute and becomes supersaturated. At a critical level new crystals begin to form, and this eases the excess so quickly that the forming of new crystals almost stops. In the last stage no new crystals appear, but the existing ones keep growing until the concentration settles back at the saturation value.

paragraphs.heading: Purifying, syrup and honey
paragraphs.text: Chemists use the effect to purify compounds, a process called recrystallization. They heat the impure compound in a solvent until it dissolves, then cool the liquid. For a short time it is supersaturated, and then the pure compound crystallizes out while the impurities stay behind in the liquid. Some substances stay supersaturated for a long time, and carbohydrates are one such class. Golden syrup, a mix of glucose and fructose, is a thick supersaturated liquid, and clear honey holds carbohydrates that may crystallize over a period of weeks.
